title: VIII. The Evidence Of The Witnesses. The Babe
paragraphs: The examination of the witnesses began. But I won't continue the story in the same level of detail as before. So I'll skip over how Nikolay Parfenovitch impressed on every witness called that he had to give his evidence according to truth and conscience, and that he would later have to repeat his testimony under oath; how every witness was required to sign the protocol of his evidence, and so on. I'll only note that the central point pressed in the examination was the question of the three thousand roubles—that is, was the sum Mitya spent here at Mokroe on the first occasion, a month earlier, three thousand or fifteen hundred? And again, had he spent three thousand or fifteen hundred the night before? Sadly, all the evidence given by every witness turned out to be against Mitya. Not one piece supported him, and some witnesses introduced new, almost crushing facts that contradicted Mitya's own account.

The first witness examined was Trifon Borissovitch. He wasn't the least bit flustered as he stood before the lawyers. On the contrary, he had an air of stern and severe indignation toward the accused, which gave him an appearance of truthfulness and personal dignity. He spoke little, and with restraint, waited to be questioned, and answered precisely and deliberately. Firmly and without hesitation, he testified that the sum spent a month before couldn't have been less than three thousand, that every peasant around here would confirm they had heard Dmitri Fyodorovitch himself mention the sum of three thousand. “The amount he threw away on the gypsy girls alone! He must have wasted a thousand on them by himself.”
“I don't believe I gave them five hundred,” was Mitya's gloomy comment on this. “It's a shame I didn't count the money at the time, but I was drunk…”
Mitya was sitting sideways with his back to the curtains. He listened grimly, with a melancholy and exhausted air, as though he were saying:
“Oh, say whatever you like. It makes no difference now.”

“More than a thousand went to them, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Trifon Borissovitch shot back firmly. “You flung it around at random and they snatched it up. They were a thieving, roguish lot, horse-stealers—they've been driven out of here, or maybe they'd testify themselves how much they got from you. I saw the sum in your hands myself—count it I didn't, you wouldn't let me, that's true enough—but by the look of it I'd say it was far more than fifteen hundred… fifteen hundred, indeed! We've seen money too. We can judge amounts…”
As for the sum spent yesterday, he insisted that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had told him, the moment he arrived, that he had brought three thousand with him.
“Come on now, is that really so, Trifon Borissovitch?” Mitya replied. “Surely I didn't declare so plainly that I'd brought three thousand?”

“You did say so, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You said it in front of Andrey. Andrey himself is still here. Send for him. And in the hall, when you were treating the chorus, you shouted straight out that you would leave your sixth thousand behind here—meaning along with what you'd spent before, that's how we're to understand it. Stepan and Semyon heard it, and Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov was standing right beside you at the time. Maybe he'd remember it…”

The evidence about the “sixth” thousand made an extraordinary impression on the two lawyers. They were delighted with this new mode of reckoning: three and three made six, three thousand then and three now made six—that was perfectly clear.

They questioned all the peasants Trifon Borissovitch had named—Stepan and Semyon, the driver Andrey, and Kalganov. The peasants and the driver confirmed Trifon Borissovitch's testimony without hesitation. They took particular care to note down Andrey's account of the conversation he'd had with Mitya on the road: “‘Where,' says he, ‘am I going, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, to heaven or to hell, and will I be forgiven in the next world or not?'”

The psychologically minded Ippolit Kirillovitch listened to this with a subtle smile, and ended by recommending that these remarks about where Dmitri Fyodorovitch would end up be “included in the case.”

Kalganov, when called, came in reluctantly, frowning and ill-humored, and he spoke to the lawyers as though he'd never met them before in his life, though they were acquaintances he'd been meeting every day for a long time. He began by saying that “he knew nothing about it and didn't want to.” But it turned out he had heard of the “sixth” thousand, and he admitted he'd been standing close by at that moment. As far as he could tell, he “didn't know” how much money Mitya had in his hands. He confirmed that the Poles had cheated at cards. In response to repeated questions, he stated that after the Poles had been turned out, Mitya's standing with Agrafena Alexandrovna had certainly improved, and that she had said she loved him. He spoke of Agrafena Alexandrovna with reserve and respect, as though she were a lady of the highest society, and he never once let himself call her Grushenka. Despite the young man's obvious reluctance to give evidence, Ippolit Kirillovitch examined him at length, and only from him learned all the details of what had made up Mitya's “romance,” so to speak, that night. Mitya never once interrupted Kalganov. At last they let the young man go, and he left the room with undisguised indignation.

The Poles were examined too. Though they had gone to bed in their room, they hadn't slept all night, and when the police officers arrived they hurriedly dressed and got ready, knowing they would certainly be sent for. They gave their evidence with dignity, though not without some uneasiness. The little Pole turned out to be a retired twelfth-class official who had served in Siberia as a veterinary surgeon. His name was Mussyalovitch. Pan Vrublevsky turned out to be an uncertified dentist. Although Nikolay Parfenovitch asked them the questions on their arrival, both of them directed their answers to Mihail Makarovitch, who was standing to one side, mistaking him in their ignorance for the most important person and the one in command, and addressed him with every word as “Pan Colonel.” Only after several reprimands from Mihail Makarovitch himself did they grasp that they had to address their answers only to Nikolay Parfenovitch. It turned out they could speak Russian quite correctly, except for their accent on certain words. Of his relations with Grushenka, past and present, Pan Mussyalovitch spoke proudly and warmly, so that Mitya was roused at once and declared he would not permit the “scoundrel” to speak that way in his presence! Pan Mussyalovitch immediately called attention to the word “scoundrel” and requested that it be entered in the protocol. Mitya burned with rage.
“He's a scoundrel! A scoundrel! You can put that down. And put down, too, that in spite of the protocol I still declare that he's a scoundrel!” he shouted.

Though Nikolay Parfenovitch did enter this in the protocol, he showed the most admirable tact and composure. After sternly reprimanding Mitya, he cut short any further inquiry into the romantic side of the case and hurried on to what was essential. One piece of testimony from the Poles aroused particular interest in the lawyers: how, in this very room, Mitya had tried to buy off Pan Mussyalovitch, and had offered him three thousand roubles to surrender his claims—seven hundred roubles down, and the remaining two thousand three hundred “to be paid the next day in the town.” Mitya had sworn at the time that he didn't have the whole sum with him at Mokroe, but that his money was in town. Mitya heatedly observed that he had not said he would definitely pay him the remainder the next day in town. But Pan Vrublevsky confirmed the statement, and after a moment's thought Mitya, frowning, admitted that it must have been as the Poles said—that he had been excited at the time and might well have said so.

The prosecutor pounced on this piece of evidence. It seemed to establish for the prosecution (and in fact they did base this deduction on it) that half, or some part, of the three thousand that had come into Mitya's hands might actually have been left hidden somewhere in town, or even perhaps somewhere here in Mokroe. This would explain the circumstance, so puzzling to the prosecution, that only eight hundred roubles were found on Mitya. Small as it was, this had been the one piece of evidence that had so far told, to some extent, in Mitya's favor. Now this single piece of evidence in his favor had collapsed. When the prosecutor asked where he would have gotten the remaining two thousand three hundred roubles, since he himself had denied having more than fifteen hundred, Mitya confidently replied that he had intended to offer the “little chap” not money, but a formal deed transferring his rights to the village of Tchermashnya—those same rights he had already offered to Samsonov and Madame Hohlakov. The prosecutor actually smiled at the “naivety of this subterfuge.”
“And you imagine he would have accepted such a deed in place of two thousand three hundred roubles in cash?”

“He certainly would have accepted it,” Mitya declared warmly. “Why, look—he could have grabbed not two thousand but four or even six out of it. He would have set his lawyers on the job, Poles and Jews, and might have gotten not three thousand but the whole property out of the old man.”

Pan Mussyalovitch's evidence was, of course, entered in the protocol in the fullest detail. Then they let the Poles go. The incident of the cheating at cards was barely touched upon. Nikolay Parfenovitch was already too pleased with them, as it was, and didn't want to trouble them over trifles—besides, it was nothing but a foolish, drunken quarrel over cards. There had been plenty of drinking and disorder that night… So the two hundred roubles stayed in the Poles' pockets.

Then old Maximov was called in. He came in timidly, approached with little steps, looking very disheveled and depressed. All this time he had taken refuge downstairs with Grushenka, sitting mutely beside her and “now and then breaking into tears over her and wiping his eyes with a blue checked handkerchief,” as Mihail Makarovitch described it afterwards. So she herself had to try to soothe and comfort him. The old man immediately confessed that he had done wrong, that he had borrowed “ten roubles in my poverty” from Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that he was ready to pay it back. When Nikolay Parfenovitch asked him directly whether he had noticed how much money Dmitri Fyodorovitch was holding—since he must have seen the sum better than anyone when he took the note from him—Maximov, in the most positive manner, declared that there had been twenty thousand.
“Have you ever seen as much as twenty thousand before, then?” Nikolay Parfenovitch inquired with a smile.

“To be sure I have—not twenty, but seven, when my wife mortgaged my little property. She'd only let me look at it from a distance, boasting about it to me. It was a very thick bundle, all rainbow-colored notes. And Dmitri Fyodorovitch's were all rainbow-colored too…”

He wasn't kept long. At last it was Grushenka's turn. Nikolay Parfenovitch was clearly apprehensive about the effect her appearance might have on Mitya, and he murmured a few words of warning to him, but Mitya bowed his head in silence, giving him to understand “that he wouldn't make a scene.” Mihail Makarovitch himself led Grushenka in. She came in with a stern and gloomy face, looking almost composed, and sat down quietly on the chair Nikolay Parfenovitch offered her. She was very pale, she seemed to be cold, and she wrapped herself tightly in her magnificent black shawl. She was suffering from a slight feverish chill—the first sign of the long illness that followed that night. Her grave bearing, her direct earnest look, and her quiet manner made a very favorable impression on everyone. Nikolay Parfenovitch was even a little “fascinated.” He admitted himself afterwards, when talking about it, that only then had he seen “how beautiful the woman was,” for though he had seen her several times before, he had always regarded her as something of a “provincial hetaira.” “She has the manners of the best society,” he said enthusiastically, gossiping about her in a circle of ladies. But this was received with downright indignation by the ladies, who immediately called him a “naughty man”—to his great satisfaction.

As she entered the room, Grushenka only glanced for an instant at Mitya, who looked at her uneasily. But her face reassured him at once. After the first unavoidable questions and warnings, Nikolay Parfenovitch asked her, hesitating slightly but maintaining the most courteous manner, what her relationship was with the retired lieutenant, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov. To this Grushenka answered firmly and quietly:

“He was an acquaintance. He came to see me as an acquaintance over the last month.” To further inquisitive questions she answered plainly and with complete frankness: that though “at times” she had thought him attractive, she had not loved him, but had won his heart as well as his old father's “in my nasty spite”; that she had seen Mitya was intensely jealous of Fyodor Pavlovitch and everyone else, but that had only amused her. She had never meant to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch, she had simply been laughing at him. “I had no thoughts for either of them this last month. I was expecting another man, one who had wronged me. But I think,” she said in conclusion, “there's no need for you to question me about that, nor for me to answer you, for that's my own affair.”

Nikolay Parfenovitch immediately took the hint. He once again set aside the “romantic” aspect of the case and moved on to the serious one—that is, to the most important question, the three thousand roubles. Grushenka confirmed the statement that three thousand roubles had certainly been spent on the first carousal at Mokroe, and although she had not counted the money herself, she had heard it was three thousand from Dmitri Fyodorovitch's own lips.
“Did he tell you that when you were alone, or in front of someone else, or did you only hear him speak of it to others in your presence?” the prosecutor asked at once.
To which Grushenka replied that she had heard him say so in front of other people, and had heard him say so when they were alone.
“Did he say it to you alone once, or several times?” the prosecutor inquired, and learned that he had told Grushenka so several times.

Ippolit Kirillovitch was very well pleased with this piece of evidence. Further questioning brought out that Grushenka also knew where the money had come from—that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had gotten it from Katerina Ivanovna.
“And did you never, even once, hear that the money spent a month ago was not three thousand but less, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had kept half of that sum for himself?”
“No, I never heard that,” answered Grushenka.
It came out further that on the contrary Mitya had often told her he didn't have a penny.
“He was always expecting to get some from his father,” Grushenka said in conclusion.
“Did he never say in your presence… casually, or in a moment of irritation,” Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly put in, “that he intended to make an attempt on his father's life?”
“Ach, he did say so,” Grushenka sighed.
“Once, or several times?”
“He mentioned it several times, always in anger.”
“And did you believe he would do it?”
“No, I never believed it,” she answered firmly. “I had faith in his noble heart.”
“Gentlemen, allow me,” Mitya cried suddenly, “allow me to say one word to Agrafena Alexandrovna in your presence.”
“You can speak,” Nikolay Parfenovitch assented.
“Agrafena Alexandrovna!” Mitya rose from his chair. “Have faith in God and in me. I am not guilty of my father's murder!”

Having said these words, Mitya sat down again on his chair. Grushenka stood up and crossed herself devoutly before the icon. “Thanks be to Thee, O Lord,” she said, in a voice thrilled with emotion, and still standing, she turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and added:

“As he has spoken now, believe it! I know him. He'll say anything as a joke or out of stubbornness, but he'll never deceive you against his conscience. He's telling the whole truth, you can believe it.”
“Thank you, Agrafena Alexandrovna, you've given me fresh courage,” Mitya responded in a quivering voice.

As for the money spent the previous day, she declared that she didn't know what sum it was, but had heard him tell several people that he had three thousand with him. And when asked where he'd gotten the money, she said he had told her that he had “stolen” it from Katerina Ivanovna, and that she had replied that he hadn't stolen it and that he must pay the money back the next day. When the prosecutor pressed her emphatically to clarify whether the money he said he had stolen from Katerina Ivanovna was what he had spent yesterday or what he had squandered here a month ago, she declared that he meant the money spent a month ago, and that was how she understood him.

Grushenka was at last released, and Nikolay Parfenovitch impulsively informed her that she could return to the town at once, and that if he could be of any assistance to her—with horses, for example, or if she'd like an escort, he… would be—

“I thank you sincerely,” said Grushenka, bowing to him. “I'm going with this old gentleman, I am driving him back to town with me, and in the meantime, if you'll allow me, I'll wait downstairs to hear what you decide about Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

She went out. Mitya was calm, and even looked more cheerful, but only for a moment. He felt increasingly oppressed by a strange physical weakness. His eyes were closing with exhaustion. The examination of the witnesses was finally over. They moved on to a final revision of the protocol. Mitya got up, moved from his chair to the corner by the curtain, lay down on a large chest covered with a rug, and instantly fell asleep.
He had a strange dream, utterly out of keeping with the place and the moment.

He was driving somewhere in the steppes, where he had been stationed long ago, and a peasant was driving him in a cart with a pair of horses through snow and sleet. He was cold, it was early November, and the snow was falling in big wet flakes, melting the moment it touched the earth. And the peasant drove him briskly; he had a fair, long beard. He wasn't an old man, somewhere around fifty, and he was wearing a gray peasant's smock. Not far off was a village; he could see the black huts, and half the huts were burned down—only the charred beams were sticking up. And as they drove in, there were peasant women lined up along the road—a lot of women, a whole row, all thin and wan, their faces a kind of brownish color, especially one at the edge, a tall, bony woman who looked forty but might have been only twenty, with a long thin face. And in her arms was a little baby crying. And her breasts seemed so dried up that there wasn't a drop of milk in them. And the child cried and cried, and held out its little bare arms, its little fists blue from the cold.
“Why are they crying? Why are they crying?” Mitya asked as they dashed cheerfully by.
“It's the babe,” answered the driver, “the babe weeping.”
And Mitya was struck by his saying, in his peasant way, “the babe,” and he liked the peasant's calling it a “babe.” There seemed more pity in it.
“But why is it weeping?” Mitya persisted stupidly. “Why are its little arms bare? Why don't they wrap it up?”
“The babe's cold, its little clothes are frozen and don't warm it.”
“But why is it? Why?” foolish Mitya kept insisting.
“Why, they're poor people, burned out. They've no bread. They're begging because they've been burned out.”

“No, no,” Mitya, still somehow not understanding. “Tell me why it is those poor mothers stand there. Why are people poor? Why is the babe poor? Why is the steppe barren? Why don't they hug each other and kiss? Why don't they sing songs of joy? Why are they so dark from black misery? Why don't they feed the babe?”

And he felt that, though his questions were unreasonable and made no sense, still he wanted to ask just that, and he had to ask it in just that way. And he felt that a surge of pity, such as he had never known before, was rising in his heart—that he wanted to cry, that he wanted to do something for them all, so that the babe should weep no more, so that the dark-faced, dried-up mother should not weep, that no one should shed tears again from that moment on. And he wanted to do it at once, at once, regardless of all obstacles, with all the recklessness of the Karamazovs.

“And I'm coming with you. I won't leave you now for the rest of my life, I'm coming with you,” he heard close beside him Grushenka's tender voice, trembling with emotion. And his heart glowed, and he struggled forward toward the light, and he longed to live, to live, to go on and on, toward the new, beckoning light, and to hurry, hurry, now, at once!

“What! Where?” he exclaimed, opening his eyes and sitting up on the chest, as though he had revived from a faint, smiling brightly. Nikolay Parfenovitch was standing over him, suggesting he hear the protocol read aloud and sign it. Mitya guessed he had been asleep an hour or more, but he didn't hear Nikolay Parfenovitch. He was suddenly struck by the fact that there was a pillow under his head, which hadn't been there when he had leaned back, exhausted, on the chest.
“Who put that pillow under my head? Who was so kind?” he cried, with a kind of ecstatic gratitude and tears in his voice, as though some great kindness had been shown him.

He never found out who this kind man was—perhaps one of the peasant witnesses, or Nikolay Parfenovitch's little secretary, had compassionately thought to put a pillow under his head—but his whole soul was quivering with tears. He went to the table and said he would sign whatever they wanted.
“I've had a good dream, gentlemen,” he said in a strange voice, with a new light, like joy, in his face.
